rows.b: The first affordable computer with a graphical screen, windows, and a mouse for ordinary buyers. What you saw on screen was what printed.
A small machine that held both its instructions and its data in the same electronic memory — the stored-program idea. Its first program, in June 1948, found the highest factor of a number.
A grid of resistors that remember their resistance, so the memory itself can do the math. Multiplying matrices happens in the wires, not in a processor.
A tiny chip with processor, memory, and input-output pins that runs a single program forever — inside toys, thermostats, and robots. It costs little and sips power.
A computer whose switches are individual molecules wired between electrodes, packing logic at the ultimate density. SPECULATION: reliable molecular circuits do not exist yet.
A processor with a clean 32-bit design inside that powered the Macintosh, the Amiga, the Atari ST, and early workstations. Programmers loved its tidy instruction set.
